# Spatially constrained vs. unconstrained filtering in neural spatiospectral filters for multichannel speech enhancement

Annika Briegleb   Walter Kellermann ^(†)^(†)thanks: This work has been
accepted to EUSIPCO 2024. Affiliation: Multimedia Communications and
Signal Processing  
Friedrich-Alexander-Universität Erlangen-Nürnberg, Erlangen, Germany  
{annika.briegleb, walter.kellermann}@fau.de

###### Abstract

When using artificial neural networks for multichannel speech
enhancement, filtering is often achieved by estimating a complex-valued
mask that is applied to all or one reference channel of the input
signal. The estimation of this mask is based on the noisy multichannel
signal and, hence, can exploit spatial and spectral cues simultaneously.
While it has been shown that exploiting spatial and spectral cues
jointly is beneficial for the speech enhancement result, the mechanics
of the interplay of the two inside the neural network are still largely
unknown. In this contribution, we investigate how two conceptually
different [NSSF](#id13) exploit spatial cues depending on the training
target signal and show that, while one NSSF always performs spatial
filtering, the other one is selective in leveraging spatial information
depending on the task at hand. These insights provide better
understanding of the information the NSSFs use to make their prediction
and, thus, allow to make informed decisions regarding their design and
deployment.

###### Index Terms: 

spatial filtering, multichannel speech enhancement, DNN interpretability

## I Introduction

\Acp

ANN used for mask-based multichannel speech enhancement, denoted as
[NSSF](#id13), can leverage spatial and spectral information jointly to
estimate the desired signal \[[1](#bib.bib1)\]. However, the interaction
between spatial and spectral filtering in these [NSSF](#id13) is still
largely unknown. Yet, understanding how, especially, spatial information
is used inside an [NSSF](#id13) would provide insights into the
proverbial black box, and allows to identify improvements and suitable
application scenarios for this specific [NSSF](#id13).

For mask-based [NSSF](#id13) that operate according to the
filter-and-sum approach and estimate one mask for each channel, e.g.,
\[[2](#bib.bib2), [3](#bib.bib3), [4](#bib.bib4), [5](#bib.bib5)\], it
can be expected that spatial filtering is indeed performed due to the
combination of all channels that enables signal phase alignment
(cf. \[[6](#bib.bib6)\]). However, in \[[7](#bib.bib7)\] the [JNF](#id8)
([JNF](#id8)) has been proposed based on \[[8](#bib.bib8)\], which uses
all channels to estimate a single-channel mask for speech enhhancement.
While spatial selectivity has been shown for the [JNF](#id8) for a
specific spatially constrained target speaker extraction scenario
\[[7](#bib.bib7)\], it is unclear whether spatial information is
extracted inside the [NSSF](#id13) for other scenarios and how the
spatial information influences the estimated mask. Thus, in the
following, we will analyze how well spatial information is represented
in the [JNF](#id8) in both spatially constrained and unconstrained
scenarios. Note that the spatial constraint will be imposed via the
training scenario of the [NSSF](#id13) and not via a constrained
optimization criterion (cf., e.g., the derivation of the [MVDR](#id12)
([MVDR](#id12)) [BF](#id2) ([BF](#id2)) \[[9](#bib.bib9)\]), or a cost
function (cf., e.g., independent vector analysis \[[10](#bib.bib10)\]).
For comparison, we will also show the spatial information represented in
an [NSSF](#id13) that uses the filter-and-sum approach, the
[COSPA](#id4) ([COSPA](#id4)) \[[2](#bib.bib2)\]. Moreover, we will
discuss the influence of two different training target signal options on
the spatial filtering behavior of both [NSSF](#id13).

Sec. [II](#S2 "II Spatially constrained vs. unconstrained filtering with NSSFs ‣ Spatially constrained vs. unconstrained filtering in neural spatiospectral filters for multichannel speech enhancement")
introduces the signal model, the spatially constrained and unconstrained
training scenarios, the training target signals, and the two
[NSSF](#id13) under consideration.
Sec. [III](#S3 "III Experimental Setup ‣ Spatially constrained vs. unconstrained filtering in neural spatiospectral filters for multichannel speech enhancement")
provides details about the experimental setup. The results are presented
and discussed in
Sec. [IV](#S4 "IV Results ‣ Spatially constrained vs. unconstrained filtering in neural spatiospectral filters for multichannel speech enhancement"),
and
Sec. [V](#S5 "V Conclusion ‣ Spatially constrained vs. unconstrained filtering in neural spatiospectral filters for multichannel speech enhancement")
concludes the paper.

## II Spatially constrained vs. unconstrained filtering with NSSFs

A signal $`X_{m}(f,\tau)`$ in the [STFT](#id17) ([STFT](#id17)) domain,
with frequency bin index $`f=1,\dots,F`$ and time frame index
$`\tau=1,\dots,T`$, captured by microphone $`m=1,\dots,M`$, is given as

|     |     |     |     |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
|     |

````math
X_{m}(f,\tau)=\sum_{q=1}^{Q}D_{qm}(f,\tau)+N_{\text{mic},m}(f,\tau).
``` |  | (1) |

$`D_{qm}(f,\tau)=G^{\ast}_{qm}(f,\tau)S_{q}(f,\tau)`$ is the signal of
speaker $`q`$ captured by the $`m`$-th microphone given as the dry
source signal $`S_{q}(f,\tau)`$ filtered by the transfer function
$`G_{qm}(f,\tau)`$ from the position of source $`q`$ to the $`m`$-th
microphone. The sum of all sources
$`q\in\mathcal{D},|\mathcal{D}|\geq 1`$, is considered as the desired
signal. $`N_{\text{mic},m}(f,\tau)`$ is the sensor noise of
microphone $`m`$. $`\mathbf{X}_{m}`$ denotes channel $`m`$ for the
entire observation interval, and the multichannel signal is denoted by
$`\mathbf{X}`$. When considering a filter-and-sum approach using the
estimated masks $`\mathcal{M}_{m}(f,\tau)`$, the estimated desired
signal $`\hat{S}(f,\tau)`$ is found as

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\hat{S}(f,\tau)=\sum_{m=1}^{M}\mathcal{M}_{m}(f,\tau)X_{m}(f,\tau).
``` |  | (2) |

When only one mask $`\mathcal{M}`$ is estimated and applied to a
reference channel, the estimated desired signal is given as

|     |                                                            |     |     |
|-----|------------------------------------------------------------|-----|-----|
|     |
       ``` math
       \hat{S}(f,\tau)=\mathcal{M}(f,\tau)X_{\text{ref}}(f,\tau).
       ```                                                         |     | (3) |

In the following, we will discuss the spatially constrained and
unconstrained scenarios which will be used to analyze the spatial
filtering behaviour of the [NSSF](#id13).

### II-A Analysis scenarios

In order to identify whether and where spatial information is
represented inside the [NSSF](#id13), the [NSSF](#id13) have to be
trained in a way that allows to uncover the spatial information
represented in their hidden features. We propose two analysis scenarios
for training. The spatially unconstrained scenario, comprises $`Q=2`$
speakers placed at two different positions in a room. There are no
constraints on the positions of the speakers except that the difference
of their [doa](#id5) $`\theta_{q}`$
(cf. Sec. [III-A](#S3.SS1 "III-A Data ‣ III Experimental Setup ‣ Spatially constrained vs. unconstrained filtering in neural spatiospectral filters for multichannel speech enhancement"))
is sufficiently large for spatially selective processing. The two
speakers are active alternatingly, hence, only one speaker is active at
any given time. This alternating activity pattern allows to associate
any time frame $`\tau`$ in a signal with the spatial information of the
corresponding active speaker. The [NSSF](#id13) will be trained to
preserve both speakers in $`\hat{\mathbf{S}}`$, i.e.,
$`\mathcal{D}=\{1,2\}`$. This scenario and training mode are chosen
purely to analyze, depending on the training target signal
(cf. Sec. [II-B](#S2.SS2 "II-B Training target signals ‣ II Spatially constrained vs. unconstrained filtering with NSSFs ‣ Spatially constrained vs. unconstrained filtering in neural spatiospectral filters for multichannel speech enhancement")),
whether the [NSSF](#id13) extract spatial information without explicitly
being told to do so.

The spatially constrained scenario is a target speaker extraction
scenario with $`Q=2`$ speakers at different positions in a room that are
active alternatingly. One of the speakers, the target speaker, will
always be positioned at a predefined fixed target [doa](#id5)
$`\theta_{\text{target}}`$ relative the microphone array. The
[NSSF](#id13) are trained to extract only the target speaker, i.e.,
$`|\mathcal{D}|=1`$. Since speaker identities change across the training
and test datasets, the [NSSF](#id13) have to learn during training which
[doa](#id5) is the desired one. Hence, the setup of the scene provides a
spatial constraint for the [NSSF](#id13).

### II-B Training target signals

Apart from the training scenario, the task of an [ANN](#id1)
([ANN](#id1)) is defined via the training target signal, i.e., the
desired signal to be estimated provided to the [ANN](#id1) during
training. For speech enhancement and target speaker extraction, the
target signal is typically the noise-free desired signal. However, this
could either be the dry source signal $`\mathbf{S}_{q\in\mathcal{D}}`$
or the noise-free signal captured by a reference microphone
$`\mathbf{D}_{q\in\mathcal{D}\text{,ref}}`$ or a processed version of
any of the two. The choice of the target signal crucially affects the
spatial filtering and the task the [NSSF](#id13) has to perform. The dry
target signal adds dereverberation to the task of the [NSSF](#id13),
while, e.g., a [BF](#id2)-filtered target signal implicitly imposes
emulating the [BF](#id2) as a task to the [NSSF](#id13).

For our investigations, we will consider the dry source signal
$`\mathbf{S}_{q\in\mathcal{D}}`$ and a [DSB](#id6)
([DSB](#id6))-filtered version of the signal
$`\mathbf{D}_{q\in\mathcal{D}}`$ (DSB target) as training target signals
for both [NSSF](#id13). We choose these two since the [JNF](#id8) has
been proposed with a dry target signal \[[7](#bib.bib7)\] and
[COSPA](#id4) has been proposed with a [BF](#id2)-filtered target signal
\[[2](#bib.bib2)\]. We choose the [DSB](#id6) as [BF](#id2) since our
focus in this paper is purely on spatial filtering. Note that when
training with the dry target signal for the spatially unconstrained
training scenario, where both speakers are considered desired speakers,
it is not necessary to exploit spatial cues to perform the task.

### II-C NSSFs

The two [NSSF](#id13) chosen for analysis differ significantly in their
architectural and conceptional design. Nevertheless, they both use
layers with memory, such as [LSTM](#id11) ([LSTM](#id11))
\[[11](#bib.bib11)\] or [GRU](#id9) ([GRU](#id9)) \[[12](#bib.bib12)\]
layers, which have already been shown to be crucial for extracting
spatial information \[[6](#bib.bib6)\]. These layers usually require
input data with two dimensions: the sequence dimension and the feature
dimension. The sequence dimension, which for time series is usually the
time axis, is not modified during processing. We will briefly review the
architectures of the two [NSSF](#id13) with focus on the layers with
memory in the following.

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Fig. 1: Architecture of the FT-JNF (adapted from \[[7](#bib.bib7)\]).
Decompression of the network output to obtain $`\mathcal{M}`$ is not
shown. The data arrangement applies to the following layer and the two
BLSTM layers only process the last two dimensions.

The [JNF](#id8) \[[7](#bib.bib7)\] shown in
Fig. [1](#S2.F1 "Fig. 1 ‣ II-C NSSFs ‣ II Spatially constrained vs. unconstrained filtering with NSSFs ‣ Spatially constrained vs. unconstrained filtering in neural spatiospectral filters for multichannel speech enhancement")
consists of two [BLSTM](#id3) ([BLSTM](#id3)) layers followed by a fully
connected layer with a hyperbolic tangent activation function. The real
and imaginary part of the complex-valued input signal are stacked for
processing (indicated by factor $`2`$ in
Fig. [1](#S2.F1 "Fig. 1 ‣ II-C NSSFs ‣ II Spatially constrained vs. unconstrained filtering with NSSFs ‣ Spatially constrained vs. unconstrained filtering in neural spatiospectral filters for multichannel speech enhancement")).
The first [BLSTM](#id3) layer uses a wide-band arrangement of the input
data, where the frequency axis is used as the sequence axis for
processing. The second [BLSTM](#id3) layer uses the time axis as the
sequence axis (‘narrow-band’ arrangement \[[7](#bib.bib7)\]). This
arrangement of the features preserves both the original time and
frequency dimensions of the input signal $`\mathbf{X}`$. We denote the
features at the input of the first [BLSTM](#id3) layer as
$`\widetilde{\mathbf{h}}_{0}`$, the features after the first
[BLSTM](#id3) layer as $`\widetilde{\mathbf{h}}_{1}`$ and the features
after the second [BLSTM](#id3) layer as $`\widetilde{\mathbf{h}}_{2}`$.
Unlike in
Fig. [1](#S2.F1 "Fig. 1 ‣ II-C NSSFs ‣ II Spatially constrained vs. unconstrained filtering with NSSFs ‣ Spatially constrained vs. unconstrained filtering in neural spatiospectral filters for multichannel speech enhancement"),
the feature vectors will be represented time frame-wise as vectors of
size $`2FM,2FU_{1},2FU_{2}`$ in
Sec. [IV](#S4 "IV Results ‣ Spatially constrained vs. unconstrained filtering in neural spatiospectral filters for multichannel speech enhancement"),
where $`U_{1},U_{2}`$ are the number of hidden units in the first and
second [BLSTM](#id3) layer respectively. The output of the fully
connected layer is decompressed according to \[[13](#bib.bib13)\] to
obtain the mask $`\mathcal{M}`$ used for estimating the desired signal
$`\hat{\mathbf{S}}`$ according to
Eq. ([3](#S2.E3 "In II Spatially constrained vs. unconstrained filtering with NSSFs ‣ Spatially constrained vs. unconstrained filtering in neural spatiospectral filters for multichannel speech enhancement")).

[COSPA](#id4) \[[2](#bib.bib2)\] consists of three building blocks,
where only the middle one, the compandor, can perform channel-dependent
processing. As depicted in
Fig. [2](#S2.F2 "Fig. 2 ‣ II-C NSSFs ‣ II Spatially constrained vs. unconstrained filtering with NSSFs ‣ Spatially constrained vs. unconstrained filtering in neural spatiospectral filters for multichannel speech enhancement"),
the compandor consists of two complex-valued fully connected layers with
a complex-valued [GRU](#id9) layer in between. We denote the time
frame-wise features before and after the [GRU](#id9) layer as
$`\widetilde{\mathbf{h}}_{\text{in/out}}(\tau)\in\mathbb{C}^{U_{\text{in/out}}}`$,
where $`U_{\text{in/out}}`$ denote the dimensionality of the features
before and after the [GRU](#id9) layer. [COSPA](#id4) estimates
$`\hat{\mathbf{S}}`$ using
Eq. ([2](#S2.E2 "In II Spatially constrained vs. unconstrained filtering with NSSFs ‣ Spatially constrained vs. unconstrained filtering in neural spatiospectral filters for multichannel speech enhancement")).

## III Experimental Setup

In
Sec. [IV](#S4 "IV Results ‣ Spatially constrained vs. unconstrained filtering in neural spatiospectral filters for multichannel speech enhancement"),
we investigate whether and where spatial information can be identified
in the [JNF](#id8), as a representative for multichannel [NSSF](#id13)
that apply single-channel masking, using the spatially unconstrained and
constrained training scenarios. For COSPA, we verify and extend the
results from \[[6](#bib.bib6)\]. We describe the experimental setup in
the following.

### III-A Data

Both scenarios are simulated using a uniform linear microphone array and
the parameters given in
Table [I](#S3.T1 "TABLE I ‣ III-B NSSFs ‣ III Experimental Setup ‣ Spatially constrained vs. unconstrained filtering in neural spatiospectral filters for multichannel speech enhancement").
We define the endfire directions of the array as $`0\degree`$ and
$`180\degree`$. All utterances are taken from the TIMIT database
\[[14](#bib.bib14)\]. For the spatially unconstrained scenario, the
training dataset named 2spk2pos-train consists of $`3000`$ sequences of
length $`7`$ s with two alternating speakers placed randomly in the room
but at least $`15\degree`$ apart from each other. Speaker 1 is active in
the first and third segment of the sequence and Speaker 2 in the second
segment. Speaker identities change across the dataset and the change in
activity happens randomly between 1 s and 3 s and 5 s and 6 s in each
sequence. The corresponding test set 2spk2pos contains $`180`$
sequences. Furthermore, we generate two more test sets with 50 sequences
each, where two different speakers are placed at the same position in
the room (2spk1pos) or one speaker is placed at two different positions
in the room (1spk2pos) to create the two sources respectively. These
test datasets allow to show that if a discrimination between the two
sources in the 2spk2pos test set is observable, it is due to spatial
information.

For the spatially constrained training scenario, the interfering speaker
is placed at least $`15\degree`$ away from the target speaker with
$`\theta_{\text{target}}=90\degree`$. The target speaker’s segment is
active for $`3`$ to $`5`$ s and can start anytime in the $`7`$ s long
sequence. The corresponding training set named 2spk2pos-1fix-train
contains $`3000`$ sequences and the test set 2spk2pos-1fix $`50`$
sequences. We generate the two test sets 2spk1pos-1fix and 1spk2pos-1fix
similarly to the unconstrained scenario with $`50`$ sequences each.

### III-B NSSFs

For the [JNF](#id8), we use $`U_{1}\!=\!256`$, $`U_{2}\!=\!128`$, an
[STFT](#id17) frame length of $`512`$ time-domain samples and a $`50\%`$
frame shift as in \[[7](#bib.bib7)\]. For [COSPA](#id4), we use
$`U_{\text{in}}\!=\!U_{\text{out}}\!=\!128`$, an [STFT](#id17) frame
length of $`1024`$ and a $`50\%`$ frame shift as in \[[2](#bib.bib2)\].
We train both [NSSF](#id13) on a [SNR](#id16) ([SNR](#id16)) cost
function \[[2](#bib.bib2)\].

|                             |                   |
|-----------------------------|-------------------|
| Number of microphones $`M`$ | $`3`$             |
| Microphone spacing          | $`0.04`$ m        |
| Room length                 | $`4`$-$`8`$ m     |
| Room width                  | $`4`$-$`8`$ m     |
| Room height                 | $`1`$-$`4`$ m     |
| Reverberation time T60      | $`0.2`$-$`0.5`$ s |
| Sampling frequency          | $`16`$ kHz        |

TABLE I: Specifications of the simulation setup.

### III-C Measuring spatial information inside NSSFs

To assess the spatial information represented in the features
$`\widetilde{\mathbf{h}}_{*}(\tau)`$, we use a discriminative analysis
via $`k`$-means clustering \[[15](#bib.bib15)\] as proposed in
\[[6](#bib.bib6)\]. If feature vectors
$`\widetilde{\mathbf{h}}_{*}(\tau)`$ contain discriminative information
about their dominant source, they should be clustered into distinct
clusters according to their dominant source. Due to the alternating
speaker activity in both training scenarios, the dominant source of any
time frame $`\tau`$ is known. We use $`k=Q+1=3`$ to provide one cluster
for each active source (which can be a speaker or speaker position) and
an additional cluster, the pause cluster, for time frames without
spatial cues, i.e., frames of silence. Clustering is performed on the
features $`\mathbf{h}_{*}(\tau)`$ which are the features
$`\widetilde{\mathbf{h}}_{*}(\tau)`$ normalized sequence-wise by
subtracting the mean and dividing by the standard deviation of the
features per hidden unit. A cluster is said to represent a source if the
majority of time frames assigned to this cluster belong to the
respective source. If, for a given sequence, both sources claim the same
cluster, the sequence is unresolved. We assess the expressiveness of the
clusters with respect to the spatial information contained in the
features using a grouping score, which measures how many feature vectors
belonging to the same source have been assigned to the same cluster. For
two sources, a grouping score of $`50\%`$ indicates no source-wise
clustering at all and a grouping score of $`100\%`$ indicates perfect
separation of the feature vectors into the two speaker clusters
according to their dominant source. Feature vectors assigned to the
pause cluster are neglected for computing the grouping score, since they
are assumed to be inexpressive with respect to spatial information.
Furthermore, we report the average percentage of unresolved sequences.
If no [doa](#id5)-dependent discrimination can be found for an
experiment, the grouping score is computed for all permutations of
source-to-cluster assignments and the highest score is kept. There are
no unresolved sequences for these cases. Since $`k`$-means clustering is
initialization-dependent, we report the results as average over five
trials with independent initialization.

## IV Results

We start by discussing the spatial information represented in both
[NSSF](#id13) for the spatially unconstrained training scenario.
Table [II](#S4.T2 "TABLE II ‣ IV Results ‣ Spatially constrained vs. unconstrained filtering in neural spatiospectral filters for multichannel speech enhancement")
confirms the results for [COSPA](#id4) from \[[6](#bib.bib6)\] for the
DSB target signal and extends them by the results for the dry target
signal. For the DSB target signal, the grouping score above $`90\%`$ for
$`\mathbf{h}_{\text{out}}(\tau)`$ indicates that the features
$`\mathbf{h}_{\text{out}}(\tau)`$ contain discriminative information
about the two sources. The high grouping score for
$`\mathbf{h}_{\text{out}}(\tau)`$ in the 1spk2pos scenario and the low
grouping score in the 2spk1pos scenario show that the discriminative
information is indeed based on spatial cues, since even the same speaker
identity can be split into the two given positions and two different
speaker identities placed at the same position can no longer be
differentiated. Hence, [COSPA](#id4) extracts spatial information from
the input signal in the spatially unconstrained scenario for the DSB
target.

| signal | dataset | \[%\] $`\uparrow`$ |  | sequences \[%\] $`\downarrow`$ |  |
|  |  | $`\mathbf{h}_{\text{in}}`$ | $`\mathbf{h}_{\text{out}}`$ | $`\mathbf{h}_{\text{in}}`$ | $`\mathbf{h}_{\text{out}}`$ |
| DSB | 2spk2pos | 69.7 | 92.9 | \- | 8$`\pm`$3 |
| DSB | 2spk1pos | 55.8 | 61.1 | \- | \- |
| DSB | 1spk2pos | 70.4 | 94.1 | \- | 3$`\pm`$2 |
| Dry | 2spk2pos | 58.7 | 76.4 | \- | 32$`\pm`$2 |
| Dry | 2spk1pos | 59.5 | 72.8 | \- | 27$`\pm`$6 |
| Dry | 1spk2pos | 57.7 | 81.1 | \- | 32$`\pm`$5 |

TABLE II: Clustering results for [COSPA](#id4) trained for the spatially
unconstrained training scenario (2spk2pos-train).

For [COSPA](#id4) trained with the dry training target, the grouping
score is lower than for the DSB target for both
$`\mathbf{h}_{\text{in}}(\tau)`$ and $`\mathbf{h}_{\text{out}}(\tau)`$,
but still exceeds $`75\%`$ for $`\mathbf{h}_{\text{out}}(\tau)`$ for the
2spk2pos test set and even reaches $`81\%`$ for the 1spk2pos test set.
The percentage of unresolved sequences is higher than for the DSB
target. It can be concluded that, while spatial information is not as
strongly represented in the features of the compandor for the dry
training target signal, it still provides some discriminative
information about the sources, even for a target signal that does not
enforce spatial filtering and for a training scenario without spatial
constraint.

The first block in
Table [III](#S4.T3 "TABLE III ‣ IV Results ‣ Spatially constrained vs. unconstrained filtering in neural spatiospectral filters for multichannel speech enhancement")
shows the evaluation metrics for the [JNF](#id8) for the spatially
unconstrained scenario and the DSB target. Since we expect that the
[BLSTM](#id3) layers are responsible for extracting spatial information,
the grouping score for the input features of the first [BLSTM](#id3)
layer $`\mathbf{h}_{0}(\tau)`$ is also provided as reference. The
grouping scores for $`\mathbf{h}_{1}(\tau)`$ and
$`\mathbf{h}_{2}(\tau)`$ are rather similar to each other, even though
the grouping score after the second [BLSTM](#id3) layer is slightly
higher for all test sets. For the 2spk2pos test set, the number of
unresolved sequences is lower for $`\mathbf{h}_{2}(\tau)`$ than for
$`\mathbf{h}_{1}(\tau)`$, indicating increased differentiability of the
two sources. The scores for the 2spk1pos and 1spk2pos test sets show
again that discriminative information is due to spatial information and
not speaker characteristics. However, the grouping score for the
2spk2pos test set is much lower than the respective score for
[COSPA](#id4), indicating that the [JNF](#id8) does not represent the
spatial information present in the multichannel input signal to its full
extent for the spatially unconstrained scencario, even with the DSB
target signal. Exemplary feature maps for this scenario and the
corresponding time-domain target signal are shown in
Fig. [3](#S4.F3 "Fig. 3 ‣ IV Results ‣ Spatially constrained vs. unconstrained filtering in neural spatiospectral filters for multichannel speech enhancement").
For the dry training target, which was the originally proposed target
for the [JNF](#id8) (third block in
Table [III](#S4.T3 "TABLE III ‣ IV Results ‣ Spatially constrained vs. unconstrained filtering in neural spatiospectral filters for multichannel speech enhancement")),
no spatial information seems to be represented in the features after the
two [BLSTM](#id3) layers, which is why reporting the results for the
2spk1pos and 1spk2pos test sets is omitted.

| U - DSB | 1spk2pos | 57.1 | 78.7 | 82.9 | 40$`\pm`$4 | 26$`\pm`$0 |
| C - DSB | 2spk2pos-1fix | 59.4 | 80.7 | 88.4 | 36$`\pm`$4 | 10$`\pm`$4 |
| C - DSB | 2spk1pos-1fix | 59.7 | 60.1 | 60.7 | \- | \- |
| C - DSB | 1spk2pos-1fix | 58.8 | 77.5 | 89.1 | 42$`\pm`$8 | 8$`\pm`$2 |
| U - Dry | 2spk2pos | 57.8 | 63.0 | 64.1 | \- | \- |
| C - Dry | 2spk2pos-1fix | 59.4 | 66.0 | 83.6 | \- | 24$`\pm`$4 |
| C - Dry | 2spk1pos-1fix | 59.7 | 61.1 | 62.6 | \- | \- |
| C - Dry | 1spk2pos-1fix | 58.8 | 63.5 | 83.8 | \- | 34$`\pm`$2 |

TABLE III: Clustering results for the FT-JNF trained for the spatially
unconstrained (U, 2spk2pos-train) and constrained (C,
2spk2pos-1fix-train) training scenarios.

Thus, while [COSPA](#id4) extracts spatial cues from the input signal
even in the spatially unconstrained scenario, the [JNF](#id8) only seems
to do so if it is enforced, e.g., by the training target. Since spatial
filtering behavior has been shown for the [JNF](#id8) for the spatially
constrained scenario in \[[7](#bib.bib7)\], we investigate next whether
the spatial information can be found in the hidden features of the
[JNF](#id8) for this scenario.

The corresponding results for the DSB training target are presented in
Table [III](#S4.T3 "TABLE III ‣ IV Results ‣ Spatially constrained vs. unconstrained filtering in neural spatiospectral filters for multichannel speech enhancement")
in the second block. Here, the grouping score for
$`\mathbf{h}_{1}(\tau)`$ for the 2spk2pos-1fix test set is higher than
for the unconstrained scenario and even higher for
$`\mathbf{h}_{2}(\tau)`$. For $`\mathbf{h}_{2}(\tau)`$, there are
significantly less unresolved sequences than for the spatially
unconstrained scenario. Hence, as expected, the features of the
[JNF](#id8) reflect more spatial information in the spatially
constrained than in the unconstrained scenario. Furthermore, while the
first [BLSTM](#id3) layer seems to be responsible for extracting the
spatial information in the spatially unconstrained scenario, the second
[BLSTM](#id3) layer increases the amount of spatially discriminative
information in the features $`\mathbf{h}_{2}(\tau)`$ significantly for
the spatially constrained scenario, which can especially be seen by the
increase of the grouping score by $`11.6`$ percentage points for the
1spk2pos-1fix test set and the strong decrease in unresolved sequences
from $`\mathbf{h}_{1}(\tau)`$ to $`\mathbf{h}_{2}(\tau)`$.
Fig. [4](#S4.F4 "Fig. 4 ‣ IV Results ‣ Spatially constrained vs. unconstrained filtering in neural spatiospectral filters for multichannel speech enhancement")
shows exemplary feature maps and the corresponding time-domain input
signal for this scenario, where the increased distinctiveness of the
features for the two sources is directly visible. For the dry target
signal (last block in
Table [III](#S4.T3 "TABLE III ‣ IV Results ‣ Spatially constrained vs. unconstrained filtering in neural spatiospectral filters for multichannel speech enhancement")),
the effect of the spatially constrained scenario on the behavior of the
[JNF](#id8) is even more drastic. While no spatial information could be
detected in the features of the [JNF](#id8) in the spatially
unconstrained scenario, the grouping score for $`\mathbf{h}_{2}(\tau)`$
is higher than $`80\%`$ for both the 2spk2pos-1fix and the 1spk2pos-1fix
test sets, which indicates clear presence of spatial information in the
features. On the other hand, no spatial information can be detected in
$`\mathbf{h}_{1}(\tau)`$. These results clearly show that the
[JNF](#id8) uses spatial information selectively based on the training
scenario and the training target signal.

## V Conclusion

We have investigated spatial filtering for two conceptually different
[NSSF](#id13): [COSPA](#id4) as a filter-and-sum approach and the
[JNF](#id8) as a multichannel approach with single-channel masking.
While it was expected that COSPA performs spatial filtering under all
circumstances due to the $`M`$ masks that are combined by the
filter-and-sum approach, it is still crucial to observe that the amount
of spatial filtering varies with the training target. For the FT-JNF, it
was unclear how the spatial information can contribute to the overall
result in the first place since it only uses a single-channel masking
approach to estimate the desired signal. Thus, it is even more important
to observe that the spatially constrained scenario forces the FT-JNF to
leverage spatial information explicitly and that the network internally
makes use of the spatial cues even though it only performs
single-channel masking. These insights into the NSSFs allow to
understand that not every so-called NSSF necessarily uses both spatial
and spectral information under all circumstances. This allows to make
informed decisions about the design and deployment of the NSSFs (e.g.,
\[[16](#bib.bib16), [17](#bib.bib17)\]) depending on the task, i.e.,
training scenario and training target signal, at hand.
````
